FIR No. 725/2005 State Vs. Mubarik Baktoo Page No. 1/30  2  CASE BRIEF i
Prosecution failed to prove the act of deception or inducement or delivery of property, as alleged.
ii Public witnesses relied on hearsay information and did not witness either of the aforesaid acts which constitute the essential ingredients of the offence of cheating.
iii Complainant was not examined as a witness during the trial.
iv Accused stands acquitted as the prosecution failed to discharge its primary burden.

1  BRIEF STATEMENT OF FACTS FOR THE DECISION:
1.
Mubarik Baktoo, a British national, stands on trial before this Court for the commission of offence of cheating in the year 2005.
By this judgment, I shall decide the case of the prosecution against the accused.

As per the prosecution version, on 14.12.2005, complainant Mr. Puente Andres Antuna, a Spanish Citizen visited Police Station Connaught Place and lodged a complaint that between 17.11.2005 to 06.12.2005 at Delhi as well as at Srinagar, accused Mubarik Baktoo cheated him (complainant) and induced him to deliver 500 US Dollars and Rs.2,88,750/ to his brother Mohd.
Rafiq Baktoo on the pretext that he will provide him 5 Star arrangements for his tour programme in India without intending to do so.

2. The complainant revealed that accused Mubarik Baktoo arranged a trip for him to Varanasi,
UttarPradesh.
He came back to Delhi after visiting Varanasi on 22.11.2005.
However, prior to his departure from Delhi to Varanasi, accused Mubarik Baktoo had assured him that he owns three other agencies in Delhi and many branches in India, U.K. and Australia.
He also told that he owns one apartment in London and one in Melbourne.
The complainant availed the services of the accused and paid 500 U.S. Dollars through American Express Travellers' Cheque No. from RC 418502993 - RC 418502997.
The accused further told the complainant to pay the balance amount to his brother in Srinagar as they also had a travel agency there.
Thereafter, the complainant flew to Srinagar where Mohd. Rafiq Baktoo received the complainant at the Airport and thereafter, put the complainant in a Hotel Boat in Dal Lake known as 'Baktoo Palace'.
In Srinagar, Mohd. Rafiq Baktoo asked the complainant to pay the balance payment of the trip.
The complainant paid an amount of Rs.2,88,750/ through card press portable machine in four installments at that time.
Thereafter, the complainant came back to Delhi on 06.12.2005 where accused Mubarik Baktoo was waiting for the complainant at the Airport.

At this stage, the complainant complained to the accused Mubarik Baktoo regarding the deficiencies in hotel room and other services at Srinagar contrary to his promises of keeping him in five star hotels.
Thereafter, the accused gave him Rajasthan and Nepal Hotel Vouchers and provided a car for whole trip in Rajasthan with effect from 16.12.2005.
On next day, the complainant again contacted the accused, however, he allegedly changed his attitude and started threatening of dire consequences.
3. On this complaint, present case FIR was registered and I.O./SubInspector Rishi Pal searched for the accused but despite best efforts, accused could not be traced out.
Hence, he was declared proclaimed offender vide order dated 06.11.2007.
Subsequently, charge sheet was filed in the concerned Court.

Thereafter, on 15.03.2014, H.C. Ajay Kumar, No. 197/CR, Central Range, Crime Branch, Delhi arrested the accused under Section 41.1 (c) Cr.PC and information in this regard was flashed to P.S. Connaught Place vide D.D. No.17A.

Thereafter, with the permission of Court,
accused Mubarik Baktoo was formally arrested in the present case and subsequently, remanded to police custody remand for one day.
The accused disclosed that he had spent all the money.

Thereafter, accused was taken to the Office of Delhi Travel Development Center at G39, Middle State vs . Mubarik Baktoo on 20 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/182414651/
2 Circle, Connaught Place whose owner, namely, Satish Kumar Mishra informed that he had closed his office about 34 years ago.

4. Subsequently, charges under Sections 174A and 420 of IPC were framed against the accused to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
5. To prove its case, the prosecution has examined 10 witnesses.
6. Shri Satish Kumar Mishra, S/o Shri S.P. Mishra, R/o E 302, Second Floor, Tagore Garden Extension, New Delhi was examined as PW1.
He deposed on oath that in the year 2005, he was running a tour and travel agency under the name and style of Delhi Travel Development Center at G39, Middle Circle, Connaught Place, New Delhi.
In the year 2005, accused Mubarik Baktoo had joined his travel agency as Assistant.

He further deposed that one Manoj Dogra had recommended the accused and he came to know that accused Mubarik Baktoo was running a travel agency under the name and style of M.M. Travels in the Outer Circle, Connaught Place.

He further deposed that on 17.11.2005, one taxi driver, namely, Chhattar Pal had brought one Spanish National Piuete Andres in his office and at that time accused Mubarik Baktoo was also present in his office.
Piuete Andres was willing to go to Varanasi and he had offered him a package for Varanasi tour which he had accepted and went to Varanasi, UttarPradesh.

However, after about 10 days, Piuete Andres again came to his office and told him that after finalizing the package of Varanasi when he went out,
accused Mubarik Baktoo contacted him outside his office and offered him a tour for Srinagar and Rajasthan and took 500 US Dollars as advance.
Piuete Andres had further told him that he was sent to Kashmir by the accused and complainant paid Rs.2,89,000/ to the accused, however, the promised services were not provided to him.
PW 1 further suggested the complainant to make a complaint against the accused as he had worked in his office for five days only and he was not aware of his whereabouts.
Later on, police also made inquiry from him and he had stated all the truth to the police.
PW1 further deposed that he came to know that accused had prepared all the documents on the papers of M.M. Travels.
He also informed the police that after 45 days from 17.11.2005, the accused stopped coming to his office and he came to know about the present incident only when Piuete Andres contacted him.
Accused present in the Court was correctly identified by PW1.

3 7. During his crossexamination, PW1 Satish Kumar Mishra deposed that Delhi Travel Development Center was his proprietorship concern which was being run from a rented accommodation at G39, Middle Circle, Connaught Place, New Delhi.
He had taken the said place on rent from Guru Nanak Motors.

He further deposed that he had not given any document relating to tenancy of the said shop to the I.O. nor any document relating to proprietorship concern.

He further deposed that tour of the complainant to Varanasi was arranged by his company through the agent/accused which was in his knowledge.

He further deposed that he had no role in the dealing between accused and the complainant regarding Kashmir Tour as the dealings had taken place outside his shop and he was not present at the spot at that time.
He did not know as to where the dealings had taken place.
He further deposed that after ten days from 17.11.2005, the complainant had made a call and told him that he had returned from Kashmir after getting the tour from them.
In reply, he had told the complainant that he was not aware about his tour of Kashmir and, therefore, asked him to come to his office.
In the meantime, the complainant might have called the driver Chhattar Pal who later on brought the complainant to his office.
PW1 was confronted with his statement MarkX where it was not so recorded.
He further deposed that complainant then narrated him the whole story.
He further deposed that police had apprehended him after few days of making of complaint by the complainant.
Thereafter, in January, 2006, whereabouts of accused were known to the police at Ashu Palace, Karol Bagh, New Delhi.
He denied the suggestion that accused was never arrested in the month of January, 2006, rather he was arrested in the year 2014.
The police took him to identify the accused where he identified him.
He further deposed that due to long passage of time i.e. 14 years, he did not remember whether police had readover his statement to him or not.
8. Head Constable Ajay Kumar, No. 197/Crime, Central Range, Crime Branch, New Delhi was examined as PW2.
He deposed on oath that on 14.03.2014 he was posted at Central Range, Crime Branch as Head Constable.
On that day, he received an information from the secret informer that one person, namely, Mubarak Baktoo, who is a proclaimed offender in the present case FIR, was present in Chuna Mandi, Pahar Ganj.
Thereafter, he passed this information to Inspector Central Range who instructed him to act upon the information.
After that he along with Head Constable Rakesh, Constable Rupesh and secret informer went to Chuna Mandi, Pahar Ganj, vide D.D. No. 11 dated 14.03.2014, copy of which is MarkA.
He further deposed that when they reached near Hotel Natraj, Yes Palace near Central Bank, secret informer pointed out towards one person and told him that the person was Mubarik Baktoo.
Thereafter, the person was over powered and apprehended.
PW2 asked about his identity but he started shouting, so he along with staff brought him to his office at Central Range, Crime Branch.
Thereafter, he made arrival entry vide D.D. No. 15 dated 14.03.2014 Ex. PW2/C.
Thereafter, he interrogated the accused and after due satisfaction apprehended/arrested him under Section 41.1 (c) of Cr.PC vide arrest memo Ex. PW2/A, bearing his signatures at point A.
The accused was personally searched vide personal search memo Ex. PW 2/B, bearing his signatures at point A.
He further deposed that a D.D. entry No. 2 dated 15.03.2014 Ex. PW2/D in that respect was also made by him.
Thereafter, he intimated Police Station Connaught Place about the arrest of accused and also informed that accused will be produced before Ld. Metropolitan Magistrate on 15.03.2014.

Thereafter, he prepared the Kalandra Under Section 41.1 (c) of Cr.PC on the basis of D.D. No. 2, Ex. PW2/E and produced accused Mubarik Baktoo State vs . Mubarik Baktoo on 20 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/182414651/

9. During his crossexamination, PW2 deposed that secret informer came to his office and gave the information.

He further deposed that after the accused was brought to his office, he interrogated him and made a D.D. entry in that respect.

He further deposed that he had never worked with accused.
He further deposed that there were about six shops in between the shop in which he was working and the shop in which the accused had his office.

He deposed on oath that on 14.12.2005, he was posted at Police Station Connaught Place and on that day, complainant Mr. Andres Puente Antuna, a Spanish Citizen came to Police Station and as per oral direction of the then SHO he made inquiry and recorded his statement.

25. During his crossexamination, PW10 Inspector Pramod Kumar deposed that on 14.12.2005 when complainant came to Police Station Connaught Place he was present there.
However, he did not remember whether he was doing on emergency duty at the said time.

He further deposed that he was not aware as to whether the complainant had lodged complaint with the Ministry or other Authorities after lodging the present complaint at Police Station Connaught Place in his presence.

27. Statement of accused was recorded under Section 218 read with Section 313 of Cr.PC on 01.02.2023.

Accused stated that he is innocent and has been falsely implicated in the present case by Satish Mishra and other tour & travel operators of Connaught Place with ulterior motives in connivance with officials of Police Station Connaught Place.
He further stated that he was never an Assistant or Associate of Satish Kumar Mishra.
He further stated that he neither cheated the complainant nor ever extended threats to him.
He further stated that complainant stayed at the House Boat 'New Baktoo Palace' at Dal Lake Srinagar and was satisfied with the services extended at the said house boat.
He further stated that all the allegations are false and concocted and have been made in connivance with Satish Kumar Mishra who is his business rival.
He further stated that he did not wish to lead any evidence in his defence.
28. Thereafter, the matter was fixed for final arguments.
29. Final arguments were advanced by Ld. APP on behalf of State as well as by Ld. Counsel for accused.
30. Ld. APP for the State submitted that the prosecution has proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and all the witnesses have invariably supported the case of the prosecution.
31. Per contra, it is submitted by Ld. Counsel for the accused that the story of the prosecution suffers from material inconsistencies and the case has not been proved beyond reasonable doubt.
It is further submitted that the complainant in this case has not been examined due to his absence and the allegations have not been substantiated.
32. The fundamental rule of criminal law postulates that the burden of proving the case rests on the shoulders of the prosecution.

The case of the prosecution is that the accused, while undertaking a tour and travel business between 17.11.2005 to 06.12.2005 at New Delhi as well as at Srinagar,
cheated the complainant Andres Puente Antuna and dishonestly induced him to deliver 500 US Dollars and Rs.2,88,750/ to his brother, namely, Rafiq Baktoo on the false pretext of providing him certain services/arrangements without ever intending to do so.
The subsequent allegation pertains to the offence under Section 174A IPC owing to the declaration of the accused as proclaimed offender.

33. Before proceeding, I may reproduce Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code for ready reference,
which reads thus:
420. Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property.
State vs . Mubarik Baktoo on 20 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/182414651/
10 --

Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
34. Section 420 IPC culminates two elements of cheating and delivery of property as a result of dishonest inducement.

Whereas the latter element is fairly clear, the former derives its meaning from Section 415 IPC, which reads thus:
415. Cheating.

Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudu lently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to de liver any property to any person, or to consent that any per son shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to "cheat".
Explanation.--A dishonest concealment of facts is a deception within the meaning of this section.
35. I may now briefly lay down the ingredients required for proving the offence under question.

For bringing home the charge under Section 420 of IPC, it is essential that - (a) The accused deceives any person by doing any act including a false representation;
(b) The deception results in dishonest or fraudulent inducement of any person to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security.

36. Thus, the offence under Section 420 IPC culminates upon proving the ingredients of deception,
followed by dishonest or fraudulent inducement and finally, the delivery of some property by any person as a result of such deceptive inducement.

Coming to the evidence led on behalf of the prosecution, it is the foremost requirement of criminal law that the prosecution must establish three essential attributes - actus reus, mens rea and causal link between the crime and accused on trial.
The actus reus required in this case is of deception and mens rea required in this case is of dishonesty or fraudulent intent.
37. The prosecution has examined ten witnesses in this case.

Apart from the police witnesses who have primarily deposed regarding the lodging of complaint, registration of FIR, arrest of the accused, preparation of seizure memo, recording of disclosure statement etc., only two public witnesses have examined by the prosecution i.e. PW1 (who was also reexamined as PW6) and PW4.

Pertinently, all the witnesses have arrived in the picture after the commission of the alleged offence.

None of the witnesses have testified to have been the principal accessories of the offence, as they neither witnessed the accused inducing the complainant, nor witnessed the failure of the accused to provide the services as promised.
Put otherwise, none of the witnesses have seen the act of deception or false promise or false representation being committed by the accused, as alleged.
39. The star witness of the prosecution is the complainant in the present case who has not been examined by the prosecution despite ample opportunities.
Despite availability, no independent public witness i.e. any employee of the house boat, hotel, driver or any neighbour has joined the investigation in the present case.
The importance of public witnesses in such cases has been highlighted time and again by the Hon'ble High Court.

40. The legal position, as settled, is that as a matter of prudence, the investigating officers must look for independent witnesses to corroborate the factum of commission of offence, the alleged cheating in this case.
The absence of any independent witnesses may not per se vitiate the entire case of the prosecution if the same can be duly explained.
41. In this case, testimony of PW1 Satish Kumar Mishra reveals that he was running a business of tour and travel which the accused also used to do prior to closure of his business.

PW1 has testified that he had no role in the dealing between accused and the complainant with respect to Kashmir Tour and the dealings took place outside his shop and he was not present at the spot at that time.
He further testified that he did not know as to where the said dealings had taken place.
PW1 further testified that complainant along with driver Chhattar Pal came to his office and narrated him whole story.
42. PW2 H.C. Ajay Kumar had just apprehended the accused after his declaration as proclaimed absconder.
PW3 Constable Rohit Yadav is mere a witness to arrest memo, personal search memo and disclosure statement.
PW4 Mahinder Kumar is a witness to the identification of photograph of accused.
Notably, the said witness never worked with the accused.
He neither visited the office of accused at any point of time nor had any direct relations with the accused.
Further, he denied any personal knowledge about accused and the present case.
43. PW8 Retired SubInspector Kapoor Singh had just recorded the FIR in the present case.
PW9 Retired Inspector Rishi Pal Sharma had testified that he had examined Satish Sharma only and no other witness was examined in his presence.
He further testified that he had gone to execute the process under Section 82 Cr.PC, however, he did not record statement of any witness while doing so.

Be it noted that it was his primary duty to execute the proclamation in the presence of some public witnesses and to record statement of neighbour or acquaintance or any public person near the place of residence of the accused.
It creates a serious doubt on the story of the prosecution.
Thus, I fail to regard the execution of proclamation order as proper and lawful.
44. PW10 Inspector Pramod Kumar testified that his role in the present case is only that he had reduced the complaint of complainant in his own handwriting.

Moreover, during his cross examination, he testified that the complainant spoke in English, but he was unable to reduce the State vs . Mubarik Baktoo on 20 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/182414651/
12 complaint in English.
Notably, he deposed that he gathered a rough idea about the complainant's grievance and did not conduct any preliminary inquiry.
He further testified that complainant never came before him after lodging the complaint on 14.12.2005.

In my considered opinion, it was the bounden duty of the SHO/IO concerned to have deputed some officials well conversant with the complainant's language in order to properly understand the grievance of the complainant and reduce the correct version in writing.

The very fact that the complaint was not recorded accurately owing to the recording witness being non conversant with the language, coupled with the fact that the complainant was never examined as a witness during the trial, demolishes the entire case of the prosecution.
45. In fact, this entire prosecution has been nothing short of a punishment for the accused.
The complainant lodged a complaint in 2005, which was reduced into writing by a recording officer who barely understood the language in which the complaint narrated the allegations.
More so, the complainant never turned up as a witness during the trial despite making efforts to engage him from Spain through video conferencing facility.
The police witnesses have testified to the procedural functions performed by them, which in itself, would be grossly insufficient to prove even one ingredient of the offence of cheating.
The two public witnesses were competitors of the accused and considering their competing business interests, they could not be said to be independent witnesses.
Be that as it may, even on merits, their testimonies are classic hearsay.

At the cost of repetition, I may note that they never witnessed the act of deception, they never witnessed the receipt of amounts by the accused, they never witnessed whether or not the services were provided by the accused as promised by him and lastly, they never witnessed the element of inducement as no amount was parted with by the complainant in their presence.
I need not say more.
46. The underlying theme behind the law of evidence is the judicial satisfaction of the Court.

There is no rigid rule of law that shuns the testimonies of police officials or even interested witnesses,
however, the evidence on record must inspire confidence of the Court and inconsistencies must be explained to the satisfaction of the Court.
Wherever judicial conscience requires due corroboration of the evidence and it is not forthcoming, the burden of proof on the prosecution falls short of a complete discharge.
In this case, even on face value, the prosecution witnesses have fallen short of proving the ingredients of the offence.
47. In this case, the prosecution has miserably failed to discharge its burden.
48. It is a cardinal principle of criminal jurisprudence that prosecution is to prove the guilt of the accused beyond the possibility of any reasonable doubt.

Although there may be an element of truth in the prosecution story against the accused but considered as a whole, there is a long distance to travel and this entire distance ought to be covered by the prosecution through legal, trustworthy and unimpeachable evidence.
Only then could an accused be convicted.

Reference could be made to the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sarwan Singh Rattan Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1957 SC 637.
49.
